Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessed domestic violence, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile unless there is some additional perpetration or morally injurious behavior by the patient during the trauma. In this profile there are no memory or threat items indicating the patient did something blameworthy during the event, so this item is clinically hard to explain.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: 'Being criticised or corrected' can occur in many PTSD presentations, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and appraisal items center on fear/safety, grief, and self-instability rather than interpersonal criticism or humiliation. Given the specified trauma and the other items selected, this trigger appears insufficiently linked to the formulation and surrounding symptoms.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For childhood witnessed domestic violence, strong self-blame can occur, but the specific wording 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with a witness-child trauma unless there is some indication she directly intervened or was held responsible. The rest of the profile does not suggest that role, so this item is clinically questionable for this trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: Avoiding open or exposed spaces implies a danger formulation centered on attack in public/exposed environments. The rest of the profile's triggers and memories are strongly interpersonal/domestic (shouting, touch, body odour, grief, visual memories of domestic violence), and the threat items emphasize checking safety/startle rather than fear of exposed outdoor space. This avoidance strategy does not fit the dominant trauma-linked threat pattern and is the least coherent item cross-node.

vignette: María was 11 when the night she saw her mother shout at a man she had never met and hear the man’s fist strike her mother’s back. The sound of the slammed door, the sudden rush of hot sweat across her own skin, and the sharp, metallic scent that followed were seared into her memory as images that flash unbidden whenever a door shuts, a body odor lingers, or someone else speaks too loudly. From that moment she began to feel a creeping dread whenever she caught her own perspiration or felt a casual touch on the arm during a police line‑up, and her brain started to label those ordinary cues as warnings that danger might be just around the corner. Those sensory triggers, in turn, pushed María toward self‑harm as a quick distraction from the swirl of images and thoughts that flooded her mind. When a coworker’s elbow brushed hers or a client’s voice rose too high, she would press a cold knife into her wrist to cut herself, hoping the sting would drown the terror. The same triggers also kept her awake at night, her eyes darting at every sudden movement, convinced that someone might break in while she slept. She would wake and stand in the dark hallway, breathing hard, and then lock herself in her car to feel a semblance of safety. The feeling that she was losing her mind—“I am going crazy”—and the belief that her own character made her vulnerable only amplified her avoidance of touch, any new face, and the slightest shift in a room’s lighting. The shame and self‑doubt María carried after the incident made her feel as though she could never trust herself to make the right call on the job. This negative appraisal made her mind seek comfort in the images of the night’s violence, but also in the certainty that staying in one seat, in one corner of the precinct, would protect her. When the memory of the shaking floor and the violent scream surfaced, she would panic and immediately run for the nearest safe seat, a habit that had now become a daily ritual at crime scenes and in interrogation rooms. The visual nature of the memory—sharp, almost photographic flashes of a broken arm and a woman's sob—was hard to recall deliberately, yet whenever she tried, the grief that followed would surge, deepening her sense that she was doomed to repeat the trauma. Her constant vigilance also fed back into her own memories. Each time she startled at a flicker of light, she would think back to that slammed door and the way her heart had pounded so hard that the walls seemed to vibrate. That reinforced the belief that the threat was real and present, and made her more likely to self‑harm in order to silence the thoughts. The self‑harm, in turn, became a marker of her fear: if she cut herself when she felt an impending danger, she believed she was proving her own helplessness. In this way, the cycle tightened: the more she tried to protect herself from a trigger, the more she convinced herself that she was doomed, and the more she relied on pain to escape the terror of the images. When María started her career as a detective, the environment that had once been a source of stability became a battlefield. On stakeouts she would refuse to sit with her partner, choosing instead the farthest bench from the vehicle’s seat, and her hesitation to let a suspect touch her hand during a questioning would cost her hours of negotiation time. Her avoidance of feeling—whether it was the thrill of a breakthrough or the sting of a reprimand—meant that she began to doubt her instincts on cases, letting her partner take the lead. The constant fear of being caught, of someone striking again, made her feel that she was losing her mind. The same self‑harm rituals that had once stopped intrusive thoughts now seemed futile, as the images she fought to silence only returned with more force when she walked into a crime scene, her senses primed to detect the familiar scent of sweat, the sound of a shout, or a sudden touch. The last months have seen María slipping further into isolation. Her partner’s offer to take a lead on a case was declined because she could not bear the thought of holding a suspect’s arm for a warrant, fearing that a touch would be a trigger. In her private life, the fear that “I am going crazy” and the shame that the incident was tied to her character have led her to avoid any conversation that could stir positive emotions; she no longer laughs at her partner’s jokes, fearing that laughter might awaken the buried terror. The cumulative effect of these patterns has left her feeling exhausted, disconnected, and terrified that she will never find peace. Her most urgent hope is that by speaking with a professional she can untangle the web of triggers, thoughts, and actions that keep her in a constant state of hypervigilance and self‑destruction, and that she will no longer feel that the night she witnessed can dictate every breath she takes.
